nameStory: The 'scarlet' in scarlet rosemallow comes from its brilliant red flowers that practically glow in wetland settings. The 'rosemallow' part reflects its membership in the mallow family, with 'rose' referring to the flower's showy, rose-like appearance rather than any relation to actual roses.
description: Scarlet rosemallow is a stunning wetland perennial that produces some of the most eye-catching red flowers you'll see in New England's wild places. This tall herbaceous plant can reach 4-8 feet in height, creating dramatic vertical splashes of color in marshes and swampy areas. The large, tropical-looking blooms seem almost too exotic for our region, yet this hardy hibiscus thrives in our wettest soils. Despite being native to the southeastern United States, it occasionally appears in New England gardens and naturalized spots.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Enormous scarlet-red flowers, 4-6 inches across, with five broad petals that feel smooth and slightly papery. The prominent central column (pistil and stamens fused together) extends out like a bottle brush and feels fuzzy to the touch.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Large, deeply divided leaves shaped like an open hand with 3-7 narrow, pointed lobes. The leaves feel smooth and slightly waxy, with prominent veining that creates a textured surface when you run your fingers along them.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall, upright herbaceous perennial reaching 4-8 feet, with sturdy stems that feel firm and slightly ridged. The plant forms impressive clumps over time, creating bold vertical statements in the landscape.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Round, papery seed capsules about an inch across that split open when ripe, releasing kidney-shaped seeds. The dried capsules make a subtle rattling sound when shaken.

habitat: In New England, scarlet rosemallow is rarely found in truly wild settings, appearing mainly in cultivated gardens, botanical collections, or occasionally naturalized near water features. When it does establish, it prefers consistently moist to wet soils in full sun, such as pond edges, rain gardens, or low-lying areas that stay damp. It thrives in the same conditions where you might find native swamp rose mallow.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as reddish shoots from the ground, with the distinctive palmate leaves unfurling. Young stems and leaves have a fresh, green scent when crushed.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season brings the spectacular scarlet flowers from mid to late summer. Individual blooms last only a day but are continuously replaced, creating weeks of stunning display.
seasonality.fall: Flowers continue into early fall, followed by the formation of round seed capsules. Leaves begin to yellow and the plant starts to die back to ground level.
seasonality.winter: Plant dies completely back to the roots, leaving no above-ground trace. Only persistent seed capsules on dried stems might remain if not cleaned up.

funFact: Despite being called 'Texas star,' this plant doesn't actually grow wild in Texas at all—it's native to southeastern swamps from Virginia to Louisiana, but somehow got saddled with the Lone Star State's name in the nursery trade!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with swamp rose mallow, but scarlet rosemallow's brilliant red flowers and deeply divided, hand-shaped leaves make it distinct from swamp rose mallow's pink or white flowers and broader, less-divided leaves. Remember: scarlet = deeply cut leaves, swamp = broader leaves.
contextualKnowledge: This southeastern native is sometimes grown in New England gardens for its dramatic tropical appearance, leading to occasional confusion about whether it's truly native to our region. The 'Texas star' common name is particularly misleading since the plant isn't native to Texas—a good reminder that common names can sometimes lead us astray geographically.
compareHints: Scarlet rosemallow stands out from its hibiscus relatives by its intense red flower color and deeply divided, almost star-shaped leaves. Swamp rose mallow has much broader, less-divided leaves and typically pink or white flowers, while rose-of-Sharon (common hibiscus) is a woody shrub rather than an herbaceous perennial. The brilliant red blooms of scarlet rosemallow are essentially unmistakable among New England hibiscuses.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Swamp rose mallow differs from the common garden hibiscus (rose-of-Sharon) by its much larger flowers, fuzzy leaves, and wetland habitat – rose-of-Sharon has smaller flowers and smooth leaves and grows in dry garden conditions.

Common hibiscus differs from its native relative swamp rose mallow by being a woody shrub rather than an herbaceous perennial, and having smaller flowers with three-lobed leaves instead of large heart-shaped ones.
Unlike its New England hibiscus relatives such as swamp rose mallow with its huge pink flowers or common hibiscus with its large shrubby form, flower-of-an-hour stays small and annual.
